1.blurb: The 1780 rebel took the name of Túpac Amaru I, the last independent Inca ruler, whom the Spanish beheaded in Cusco's main square in 1572. The Inca story tells that ending — and how the conquest of Pizarro's generation broke the empire whose memory the eighteenth-century revolt tried to summon back to life.

The Spanish silver-mine draft was a brutal twist on a genuine Inca institution. The Inca state ran on the mit'a, a rotating community labor levy that built its roads, terraces, and storehouses and farmed state land — a reciprocal duty, not chattel slavery. The Inca chapter on the imperial machine shows how that system worked before the Spanish redirected it to kill men in the mines of Potosí.

Spain assembled its American empire by toppling the two great Indigenous states it found there. The Inca narrative tells the conquest from the other side — Pizarro at Cajamarca, the seizure of Atahualpa, and the long, bloody dismantling of the largest empire the Americas had ever produced, the foundation on which the Viceroyalty of Peru was built.

The other half of Spain's conquering surge. The Aztec narrative tells how Cortés and his Indigenous allies brought down Tenochtitlan in 1521, the fall that created New Spain — the richest and most populous of the viceroyalties, and the future Mexico whose two-stage revolution this book follows.

The casta system this chapter calls the social fuel of independence was invented in the century after the conquest. Age of Exploration Ch 14 ("The World the Voyages Made") shows it being built — Spain's almost mathematical mania for sorting Spanish, Indigenous, and African ancestry into ranked categories — and names it one of the voyages' ugliest and most durable legacies. This chapter is where that legacy finally detonates.

The Potosí silver and the mita that fed it — the extraction engine independence leaders attacked as colonial theft — are the subject of Age of Exploration Ch 11 ("The Silver Engine"). The new narrative shows the colonial economy this chapter inherits being installed: the mine, the forced labor draft, and the bullion flow that made the colonies, by the crown's design, a thing to be drained.

2.blurb: The slave-trade narrative devotes a whole chapter to Haiti — 'the revolution that couldn't happen' — tracing how the most profitable slave colony on earth became the one place where the enslaved overthrew the system entirely. It is the deeper account of the death machine sketched here: the sugar economy, the Middle Passage that fed it, and why Saint-Domingue's revolt terrified every slaveholder in the Atlantic world.

The arithmetic that made the Caribbean a death machine is laid out in full in the slave-trade narrative's chapter on the plantation complex and its economics — why it was cheaper to work an enslaved person to death and buy a replacement than to keep one alive, and how that calculation built the wealth of France and Britain on the bodies of the people who rose in 1791.

2.blurb: The Caribbean death-machine-versus-mainland contrast this chapter draws is built out in full in Atlantic Slave Trade Ch 2 ("The System Scales: Brazil and the Caribbean"): why the sugar islands worked enslaved people to death and bought replacements while North American slavery grew by birth, and what that demographic difference meant for the shape of slavery in each place.

3.blurb: Brazil was Portuguese in the first place because of a line drawn on a map in 1494. The age-of-exploration narrative tells how the Treaty of Tordesillas split the unexplored world between Spain and Portugal along a meridian in the Atlantic — handing Portugal the eastern bulge of South America, the colony its king would flee to three centuries later.

7.blurb: The mountain of silver that the independence leaders attacked as the engine of colonial theft was, in the conquest era, the engine of the entire Spanish world economy. The age-of-exploration narrative's chapter on the silver engine shows how Potosí's bullion financed Spain's European wars, drove global trade all the way to China, and was dug under the deadly mita draft inherited from the Inca.

8.blurb: Mexico's beloved brown-skinned Virgin, whose banner Hidalgo's rebels carried, rose from the wreckage of the Aztec world the Spanish conquered. The Aztec narrative tells the fall of Tenochtitlan and the Indigenous society that Catholicism was grafted onto — the deep past that made the Guadalupe cult, and Mexican identity itself, a fusion of conquered and conqueror.

Guerrero's 1829 abolition of slavery alarmed the American settlers in Mexico's northern province of Texas and helped set off the chain of events that cost Mexico half its territory. The antebellum-America narrative tells that story from the United States' side — Manifest Destiny, the Texas revolt, and the expansionist hunger that pulled the border ever southward.

The war that tore away California, the Southwest, and the rest of Mexico's north is told in full from the American side in the antebellum narrative's chapter on the Mexican War — the 1846–48 conflict that nearly doubled US territory and reopened the slavery question that would split the Union.

9.blurb: Brazil received more enslaved Africans than any other destination in the Atlantic trade — far more than the United States — and clung to slavery longer than any country in the hemisphere. The slave-trade narrative's chapter on the afterlife and the reckoning weighs that scale and its long shadow, the human foundation under the slaveholding empire Pedro I built.

9.blurb: Brazil was the Atlantic trade's largest single destination and its last holdout. Atlantic Slave Trade Ch 9 ("The Slow Legal End") tells the long, staged road to the 1888 Golden Law — the Law of the Free Womb, the British pressure, the enslaved abolishing slavery with their feet — and sets Brazil's 1888 abolition at the end of the hemispheric sequence that ran Britain 1833, the United States 1865, Brazil last.

11.blurb: Brazil's slow, grudging abolition was driven partly by a global campaign that had begun decades earlier and an ocean away. The slave-trade narrative's chapter on the abolition movement traces how a once-unthinkable idea — that the trade and then slavery itself must end — became British state policy and then an irresistible international pressure that reached even the last great slave society in the Americas.

Brazil's 1888 'Golden Law' was the very last act in the legal dismantling of Atlantic slavery. The slave-trade narrative's chapter on the slow legal end tells the whole drawn-out process — the trade bans, the free-womb laws, the emancipations across the hemisphere — of which Brazil's uncompensated abolition was the closing chapter, nearly a century after Haiti.

The 1823 declaration that Europe must keep its hands off the Americas is told from the United States' side in the early-republic narrative's chapter on the Era of Good Feelings — a bold-sounding warning issued by a minor power with no navy to enforce it, riding entirely on British sea power, that would only grow teeth as the United States became the industrial giant that pulled Panama away from Colombia in 1903.
